title: Junior Account Manager
description: JOB PURPOSE : We are seeking an ambitious and commercially minded Junior Account Manager to join our Sales team and support the management of key national retail accounts. Reporting to the National Account Manager, you will play an integral role in analyzing sales data, developing strategic customer partnerships, driving profitable sales growth, and delivering exceptional customer service across a portfolio of grocery/retail customers. The ideal candidate for this role will have sales analytics experience within the consumer/beauty product industry. In addition, this individual will support smaller grocery accounts working closely with the National Sales Manager to whom the position reports. This role provides an excellent opportunity to develop a career in Account Management. You will work collaboratively with internal teams including Marketing, Category, Supply Chain, Finance, Customer Service, and Demand Planning to execute customer strategies, deliver business objectives, and support the continued growth of our wholesale retail partnerships. ESSENTIAL FUNCTIONS : Achievement of targets . Monthly, quarterly, annual sales and profit targets. Ensure flawless implementation of all new product development and achievement of required distribution objectives. Responsibility for the development , maintenance, and implementation of all administration. Preparing reviews for all accounts within his/her responsibility, including strategic planning and resource allocation to achieve account objectives. Build multi-level contacts and develop productive business relationships with external customers Manage and control all promotion expenditure within your responsibility in line with the companyâs guidelines, to ensure an optimum return on investment. Develop and improve tools and systems to monitor the marketplace, our brands and competitorâs performance. Effectively collaborate and coordinate activity within internal departments , category, customer marketing, finance, and customer services to deliver companyâs business priorities. Own and drive initiatives which deliver improved levels of customer service and satisfaction. Responsibility for ensuring identified expenses are kept within budgeted guidelines and completed on time as required by company policy. Ensure personal developments by implementing agreed training and development objectives Drive Off-Shelf Promotional Programs to increase sales through off-shelf promotional programs by developing profitable display features and winning feature space within retailer opportunities Implement Holiday Program to grow sales and profit through Global Sourcing initiative. Pursue opportunity to expand sales in Seasonal category by developing optimal offering, navigating online bid process, guide organization through retailer requirements and timeline of direct import program. Share and Leverage Category Success Stories . Serve as âthought leadershipâ to the PPI Trade Marketing & Sales organization by regularly share product / category success stories to use with other retailers to drive incremental sales across the organization. Identify business opportunities through collaboration and optimize profitability through negotiation with retailer and FBB Marketing / PD organization. Translate those business opportunities into account-specific strategies and tactics that drive market share and growth. Integrate and analyze multiple data sources to create strategies and programs that deliver win-win outcomes through innovation and collaboration with the account team Connect, develop, and maintain relationships with key Retailer Organization contacts, including Buyers, Merchants, Modular Development, Replenishment, Transportation, and Logistics. Cultivate account relationships to understand customer needs and goals to capitalize on business opportunities Build rapport , communicate strategy, and negotiate with customer decision makers, resulting in increased distribution, shelving, merchandising, and improved marketing of FBB brands. Analyze sales trends and supply chain efficiencies to make recommendations to maximize opportunities, while analyzing forecasting metrics and data to ensure accuracy targets are met. Track and report monthly forecast versus actual POS reports, pro-actively addressing potential issues with logistics and inventory levels using monthly key performance indicators (fill rate, in-stock % and carrier on-time %). QUALIFICATIONS: Bachelor's degree in business, commerce, marketing, or related discipline Minimum 2-3 yearâs experience in account management, sales analysis and support, customer management, or FMCG/consumer goods sales Experience working with major retail grocery chains, wholesale customers, military or distributors Knowledge of retail sales reporting, category management principles, and promotional planning Proactive, collaborative, and adaptable, with a commitment to delivering outstanding customer outcomes Familiarity with syndicated market data (such as Circana/IRI or NielsenIQ) is an advantage Strong commercial awareness and an interest in developing a career in Key Account Management Strong organizational skills with the ability to manage multiple priorities and meet deadlines Special skills required: Open and accessible communication style, with the ability to consistently achieve positive results Comprehensive knowledge of the consumer products industry, the category, brand strategies, competitors, classes of trade, with the ability to apply this knowledge to solve complex problems successfully High level of proficiency in Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Microsoft Office Excellent oral and written communication skills Ability to develop and share business presentations Strong analytical skills with the ability to interpret sales data and translate insights into recommendations Excellent people skills with the ability to work well across cross functional teams. Passion for the products and business Results-oriented with a constant sense of urgency; think like an owner and be curious Thrives in a fast-paced environment, while maintaining an enthusiastic hunger for business A valid driver's license and willingness to travel to customer locations when required. What We Offer Competitive salary and annual performance incentive Professional development and mentoring from experienced National Account Managers Career progression opportunities within Key Account Management and Sales Leadership A collaborative, high-performing team environment Employee product discounts and wellbeing initiative. Comprehensive benefits package, including paid leave and health benefits Equal Opportunity Employer We are committed to fostering an inclusive workplace where everyone is treated with respect and can succeed. raw.description:
We are seeking a Social Media Strategist to build and grow a personality-led social media presence from the ground up.

This is a hands-on, end-to-end role covering strategy, account setup, content planning, production management, publishing, audience growth, community management, and performance optimization across Instagram and TikTok. You will work closely with the founder to establish a distinctive online identity and develop it into a recognizable, highly engaging social presence.

Responsibilities

  • Build and launch the Instagram and TikTok profiles from zero, including positioning, tone of voice, content pillars, visual direction, and channel strategy
  • Develop and execute the organic growth strategy, with a focus on reach, engagement, follower growth, and long-term audience development
  • Create viral campaign concepts, social-first stories, and repeatable content formats that establish a distinctive and recognizable online personality
  • Manage the full content lifecycle, including research, ideation, scripting, content calendars, production coordination, approvals, publishing, and optimization
  • Use platform analytics, audience insights, watch time, retention, and engagement data to guide creative decisions and improve performance
  • Manage day-to-day community engagement and coordinate with the founder and creative partners


Requirements

  • Proven experience launching and organically growing Instagram and TikTok accounts from an early or zero-follower stage
  • A strong portfolio of high-performing, viral, or culturally relevant social content supported by measurable growth results
  • Deep understanding of Instagram and TikTok algorithms, audience behavior, retention, discoverability, engagement, and organic growth mechanics
  • Strong creative strategy and social-first storytelling skills, with the ability to turn a personality into compelling and repeatable content
  • Hands-on experience managing social media end to end, from strategy and content development through production, publishing, analytics, and community management
  • Strong project management and collaboration skills, with the ability to work closely with the founder and creative production partners
  • Able to work PST hours


Nice to Have

  • Experience working with creator-led brands, founders, entertainment properties, personality-driven accounts, legal brands, or character-led content is advantageous but not required

description: 30+ Engineering Career Ladders Before jumping into the list, let's quickly discuss software engineering career ladders. We can extract common traits from those career ladders; understanding those characteristics allows us to connect the dots more easily and compare different career ladders efficiently. What Is a Career Ladder? A career ladder, or career path, is a progression framework. It allows an organization to describe the different job levels and the expectations for a given position. It enables the assessment of a software engineer's skills and to work on her career progression. It provides a shared framework to identify the different aspects to improve to reach the next job level. The ladder can also be mapped with employee's compensation, increasing salaries transparency, and fairness. Expertise Path and Manager Path (Dual-Track) Most of the software engineering career ladders are dual tracks ladders. They have a joint base for the first positions, and at some point, two paths are possible the expertise path and the people management path. The expertise path is often named the individual contributor track, the people management path is often called the manager track. The career path depends on the stage of the company and the size of the team. New positions will usually appear while the engineering group is growing. Example for a tiny team (up to 10 engineers) You'll rarely find ladders at that scale; it's still very early stage, the team is a handful of engineers working with a CTO or a Tech Lead. In startups, the engineering lead is often the technical Co-founder and CTO. Single Track Notes Engineer Creating solutions to business problems Senior Engineer Handling most complex parts and mentoring Engineering Lead She may handle people management aspects At this stage, it's pretty common to have one lead developer or engineering lead who owns technical guidance and organizes the team's delivery. She is often more focused on delivery and does not handle people management which a founder still handles. Example for a small team (~20 engineers) At that point, the company will introduce middle management positions, usually an Engineering Manager (EM) position. The EM supports a group of 5 to 10 engineers, especially on human resources and project management aspects (ex: hiring, onboarding, organizing, coaching, delivery plan, reporting). In some companies, EM can be very hands-on on the system part and provide technical and architecture guidance, playing both technical leader and people/team leader. Usually, the company starts to split tech guidance and people management; both require significant and specific expertise. The company has usually introduced the role of Head of Engineering, Engineering Director, or VP Engineering. This role is about leading the whole engineering department; the engineering managers will report the person having this role. Leadership has usually introduced another new role to support the technical guidance at a broader scale, for the whole system or a large part of the system. 30+ Engineering Career Ladders

Before jumping into the list, let's quickly discuss software engineering career ladders. We can extract common traits from those career ladders; understanding those characteristics allows us to connect the dots more easily and compare different career ladders efficiently.

What Is a Career Ladder?

A career ladder, or career path, is a progression framework. It allows an organization to describe the different job levels and the expectations for a given position.

It enables the assessment of a software engineer's skills and to work on her career progression. It provides a shared framework to identify the different aspects to improve to reach the next job level.

The ladder can also be mapped with employee's compensation, increasing salaries transparency, and fairness.

Expertise Path and Manager Path (Dual-Track)

Most of the software engineering career ladders are dual tracks ladders.

They have a joint base for the first positions, and at some point, two paths are possible the expertise path and the people management path. The expertise path is often named the individual contributor track, the people management path is often called the manager track.

The career path depends on the stage of the company and the size of the team. New positions will usually appear while the engineering group is growing.

Example for a tiny team (up to 10 engineers)

You'll rarely find ladders at that scale; it's still very early stage, the team is a handful of engineers working with a CTO or a Tech Lead. In startups, the engineering lead is often the technical Co-founder and CTO.

Single Track Notes Engineer Creating solutions to business problems Senior Engineer Handling most complex parts and mentoring Engineering Lead She may handle people management aspects

At this stage, it's pretty common to have one lead developer or engineering lead who owns technical guidance and organizes the team's delivery. She is often more focused on delivery and does not handle people management which a founder still handles.

Example for a small team (~20 engineers)

At that point, the company will introduce middle management positions, usually an Engineering Manager (EM) position. The EM supports a group of 5 to 10 engineers, especially on human resources and project management aspects (ex: hiring, onboarding, organizing, coaching, delivery plan, reporting).

In some companies, EM can be very hands-on on the system part and provide technical and architecture guidance, playing both technical leader and people/team leader. Usually, the company starts to split tech guidance and people management; both require significant and specific expertise.

Individual Contributor (IC) Track People Manager Track Engineer - Senior Engineer - Tech Lead Engineering Manager

Example for a medium team (50+ engineers)

You'll start to have more levels and more expert positions at that stage. The company has usually introduced the role of Head of Engineering, Engineering Director, or VP Engineering. This role is about leading the whole engineering department; the engineering managers will report the person having this role.

Leadership has usually introduced another new role to support the technical guidance at a broader scale, for the whole system or a large part of the system. This role can be named Staff Engineer, Principal Engineer, etc.

Individual Contributor (IC) Track People Manager Track Engineer - Senior Engineer - Tech Lead Engineering Manager Staff Engineer VP Engineering

Example for a large team (100 to 1000+ engineers)

At this stage, the engineering department will create a lot of new intermediary positions to capture the level of expertise and area of ownership and impact. Welcome to Senior Engineer I and II, Engineering Director, etc.

title: Rent the Runway
description: Mar 26 Mar 26 Sharing Our Engineering Ladder Camille I gave a talk last year at the NYC CTO summit on how and why to introduce structure into an engineering organization (slides available here). I am a fan of structure and the clarity that it can provide an organization, despite its potential downsides. I'm not going to talk about the WHY very much in this post, but I thought it was about time that I helped with the HOW. Creating an engineering ladder (that is, the job descriptions and levels of an engineering organization) is a daunting task. If you do a half-hearted job, you're likely to cause more problems than you solve. The very first ladder I presented to my team was based on the ladder at Foursquare*. It was very simple, with one or two descriptive elements per "attribute" of engineering (technical skill, communication skill, etc), and by all accounts worked very well for their team. I hoped that this style of providing fewer details would result in people being less obsessed with the ladder, less likely to try to negotiate their level on "technicalities". Boy was I wrong. Almost immediately I had engineers debating me over whether they were at the right level, and there was a great deal of anxiety and confusion throughout the organization. I left room for generous interpretation, and it made it difficult for me to explain what I really wanted and expected. In addition to the ladder causing problems inside of my team, we were having a hard time evaluating candidates during interviews and determining what level to hire them into. Particularly at the more senior levels, it wasn't clear what the criteria for success really looked like. So, together with my tech leads and engineering managers, we rewrote the ladder to be more specific. It has been very helpful both for the process of reviews and promotion committees as well as for the process of hiring. I have since shared my ladder privately with several engineering managers around the country who were looking for inspiration, and today we're making it public for the benefit of all. I'm sharing this ladder not to suggest that it is the be-all end-all of engineering ladders, but to give you what I hope is a more thorough starting point than you might have seen elsewhere. After all, no one is really writing these ladders from scratch, whether we pull directly from other companies (as this one does at points), or indirectly from our past experience, so the more data points the merrier. Without further ado, I present our engineering ladder, in both spreadsheet, and long-winded text, warts and all. Please feel free to clone this ladder and update it for use in your own organizations. A special thanks to Harry Heymann, Jason Liszka and Andrew Hogue, authors of the original Foursquare eng ladder!
